what: A vector database stores embeddings - lists of numbers that capture meaning - and finds the stored items closest in meaning to a query, not just exact word matches.
like: Like a librarian who knows which books feel alike, so asking for 'sad space movies' still finds 'lonely astronaut stories'.
why: Powers semantic search, RAG for chatbots and recommendations
Finds similar items in milliseconds even across millions of vectors
Combines with metadata filters and keyword search for precise results

steps.d: Split content into chunks and run each through an embedding model. Similar meanings end up as nearby points.
Comparing a query with every vector is slow at scale, so the database builds an approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) index such as an HNSW graph.
The question goes through the same embedding model, so it lands in the same space as the content.
The search hops through the graph towards closer and closer points, checking only a small part of the data.
Metadata filters keep results inside the right tenant or date, and an optional reranker orders the final few by relevance.

choices.d: HNSW gives better speed for the same recall but builds slower and uses more memory; IVF builds fast with less memory but searches less efficiently.
Looking at more candidates raises recall (finding the true nearest) and costs time. Tune it on real queries.
Use what your embedding model was trained for - usually cosine; also L2 or inner product. pgvector writes them as <=>, <-> and <#>.
Mix vector results with keyword (BM25) results so exact names, codes and rare words are found too.

instead.why: Exact keyword and full-text search, filters and facets
pgvector keeps vectors next to your rows in one database
Blends vector and keyword search into one ranked list

breaks.t: Results changed after adding an index
breaks.d: Approximate indexes trade a little recall for speed, so some true neighbours can be missed.
breaks.see: Fewer or different matches than an exact search on the same query
breaks.fix: Raise ef_search or probes; measure recall against exact search on a sample

breaks.d: Filtering after the approximate search can drop most candidates.
breaks.fix: Search more candidates, use iterative or filtered index scans, or partition by tenant

breaks.d: Vectors from different models live in different spaces and cannot be compared.
breaks.see: Relevance suddenly drops after a model upgrade
breaks.fix: Re-embed everything into a new index, then switch over in one step

breaks.d: Embeddings capture meaning, so rare codes and product names can rank low.
breaks.see: Searching an order number or SKU finds nothing useful
breaks.fix: Add keyword search and merge both result lists (hybrid search)

say: Documents are chunked and embedded once; queries use the same model so both live in one vector space.
I use an HNSW index for fast approximate search, and tune ef_search until recall on a test set is good enough.
Every vector carries tenant and date metadata, and I filter on it so one customer never sees another's data.
For names and codes I add keyword search and merge the two lists, then rerank the top results.

followups.q: How do you know the search is good enough?
followups.a: Build a small set of real queries with known good answers, then measure recall@k against an exact search and track it as you tune ef_search or change models.

followups.q: How do you upgrade the embedding model?
followups.a: Embed all content with the new model into a fresh index alongside the old one, test it, then switch traffic over at once - mixed vectors are not comparable.

followups.q: Why not just compare against every vector?
followups.a: Exact search reads everything, which is fine for small sets but too slow at millions of vectors. ANN indexes check a small part of the data and still find almost all true neighbours.

check.q: Which index gives better search speed for the same recall in pgvector?
check.why: HNSW wins on speed versus recall, at the cost of slower builds and more memory.

check.q: After adding an approximate index, results differ slightly. Why?
check.a: It trades a little recall for speed
check.why: Approximate indexes skip most of the data, so they can occasionally miss a true neighbour.

check.q: You switched to a new embedding model. What must you do?
check.a: Re-embed all content with the new model
check.why: Different models produce different spaces, so old and new vectors cannot be compared.

check.q: Searches for exact product codes find nothing. Best fix?
check.why: Hybrid search catches exact terms that meaning-based vectors may rank low.
